title: Halifax Police treating death of inmate as homicide
article: The death of an inmate found in his cell at a Nova Scotia jail early Monday is being treated as a possible homicide, police said Monday.
The body of the 22-year-old was found at about 6:15 a.m. by staff at the Central Nova Scotia Correctional Facility in Burnside, near Halifax.
The cause of death wasn't known.

"There is an autopsy scheduled for (Tuesday) and we won't be identifying the man's name until, first of all, that this is a homicide and, secondly, that his next of kin has been notified," said Constable Jeff Carr, a police spokesman.
The Nova Scotia Medical Examiner Services and provincial Justice Department were also investigating.
The man was in a cell that housed two inmates, provincial Justice Minister Cecil Clarke told CTV News.
"I don't have any information to determine what the relationship of the two men might have been or if they knew each other," said Mr. Clarke.
The justice minister said the cells are checked "on average" every 30 minutes by a correctional officer.
Last year, the union that represents correctional officers was critical of the Tory government for permitting the double bunking of prisoners at the provincial jail.
Meanwhile, RCMP continued to investigate the unrelated death of a man who was being held in custody at a police station in Enfield, N.S., over the weekend.
Police said the man appeared to be sleeping in his bunk during regular checks throughout the night, but he was found dead in his cell on Sunday morning.
Ryan Allen McKay, 28, of Waverley, N.S., was arrested at a residence at about 9 p.m. Saturday for allegedly breaching a court order.
RCMP Sergeant Mark Gallagher said Mr. McKay was co-operative and behaving normally with officers when he was placed in a cell at the force's Enfield detachment.
He was found dead in his bunk about seven hours later.
"From the time they picked him up to the time they noticed he was non-responsive, everything appeared normal," Sgt. Gallagher said.
"There didn't seem to be anything medically that would lead them to believe they should have called an ambulance at his residence."
Although suicide hadn't been ruled out, there were no obvious signs that Mr. McKay took his own life, Sgt. Gallagher said.
There were also no outward indications he was impaired or on drugs, the officer added.
Sgt. Gallagher said officers at the detachment checked on Mr. McKay throughout the night as he lay in his bunk and appeared to be sleeping.
An autopsy was performed Monday but there was no immediate word on the results.
Halifax Regional Police have been asked to investigate the death with the assistance of the RCMP.
